Works

Installation and performance, 2023–2026

Performative installation in the Aula Hall, Academy of Fine Arts Vienna. Curated by Yein Lee.Video

Medium
Performative installation
Components
Acrylic mirrors, white-noise machine, porcelain plates and coffee cups, smoke detector, three wooden sculptures
Dimensions
Variable, site-responsive
Exhibition
Satellite solo exhibition of the group exhibition In the Fold of the Sack

Staged in the historic Aula of the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, Fans, Fans disperses acrylic mirrors, porcelain plates and coffee cups, a white-noise machine, a smoke detector, and three wooden sculptures across a monumental floor. Reflection turns the institution back onto itself while domestic fragments meet ceremonial architecture. Comfort and surveillance operate on the same surface, producing an atmosphere in which human presence is held, watched, and quietly managed.

Performative installation. Solo exhibition at 1AO SPACE, Seoul, curated by Jinseo Park.Documentation

Medium
Performative installation
Components
Sculptural structures, moving image, interface graphics, sound
Dimensions
Room-scale, approx. 16 m²
Performance
Gaeun Lee

Taking the EA FIFA video game series as a point of departure, freekick, non-freekick examines how football culture converts the body into a readable and tradable unit. Player ratings, interface graphics, scores, and repeated gestures organize the installation as an economy of comparison and metric control. Bodies and technical systems do not simply reflect one another; they actively produce one another through display and spectatorship.

Video installation. A video essay on the body-shaming of Kim Jong Un.Video

Medium
Video installation
Components
Folding screen, projection, acrylic mirror, sound, white-noise machine
Duration
7 min, HD
Dimensions
Folding screen (paravent), 1.3 × 2.4 m (H × W)

near the well is a seven-minute video essay projected onto a folding screen and doubled by an acrylic mirror, accompanied by continuous white noise. Taking the intensified body-shaming of Kim Jong Un as one of its entry points, the work traces how a figure named evil through his violence is then stabilized as a consumable image, as political condemnation slides into caricature, ridicule, and visual simplification.

The body becomes one of the media’s most efficient surfaces, onto which fear, disgust, hatred, and moral certainty can be projected at once. Shape-shaming appears not as an isolated insult but as one axis within a broader machinery of demonization. Projection, reflection, furniture, and sound form an apparatus in which the body appears only after being filtered through media and display.

Performative installation. Work in progress, to be exhibited in Seoul in 2027.

Medium
Performative installation
Components
Two IKEA furniture pieces, wooden sculpture, uncooked rice
Status
Work in progress
Exhibition
Seoul, 2027

In aftercrop, two IKEA furniture pieces are opened, tipped over, and stacked with a wooden sculpture, while uncooked rice settles in an open drawer. A loaf of bread rests on the head of a floor lamp. Staple food and flat-pack furniture meet as parts of the same domestic supply system.

Machinima video installation in an underground parking garage, Mainz.Video

Medium
Machinima video installation
Components
PVC scaffolding net, projection, sound, humidifier
Dimensions
Variable, site-responsive

happymeal projects a machinima environment onto PVC scaffolding net in a subterranean parking space in Mainz. Chickens, pigs, and cattle move through rendered barns, transport cages, and feeding lines while the net acts simultaneously as fence, filter, and screen. The surrounding concrete, artificial light, and ventilation extend the barn into the underside of the city, revealing care, capture, and consumption as parts of one continuous logistical surface.

Performative installation, co-authored with Sophie Berghäuser, Edvard Vellevoog and Tamuna Gochashvili. Lombardi—Kargl, Vienna.

Medium
Performative installation
Authors
JH Gim, Sophie Berghäuser, Edvard Vellevoog, Tamuna Gochashvili
Context
Together with Wendelien van Oldenborgh and the Concept Class, Academy of Fine Arts Vienna
Venue
Lombardi—Kargl, seventeenjoy project space, Vienna

Equinox was made for 17(Joy) Intermission: Joy as Resistance at Lombardi—Kargl, Vienna. A smartphone camera interface is projected across a gridded surface through which a performer, wrapped in plastic, is seen lying below, so that the body appears through the controls of the device that records it.

At her grandmother’s funeral, Mijin reunites with her mother after a long separation. While sorting through her grandmother’s belongings, fragments of a past summer begin to return. The presence of the frogs she once caught starts to permeate the present landscape, and Mijin moves slowly between the dead and what remains.

Single-channel video, 8'44". Seoul and Mainz.Watch film

Format
Single-channel video, color, sound
Duration
8'44"
Context
Seoul / Mainz

A Korean family’s online worship is interrupted by an unknown error. From that rupture, ohayo drifts through blue skies, kebabs, and the hidden logic of a cactus positioned by the window. Domestic belief, interface failure, and more-than-human observation fold into one another as the home becomes shrine, screen, and malfunctioning system. The plant is not a decorative object but a witness that changes how the household can be perceived.

Collaborations

Video direction

Video director for an interdisciplinary theatre work, 70'30". Art Space Mullae, Seoul.

Role
Video director
Format
Interdisciplinary theatre, 70'30"
Venue
Art Space Mullae, Seoul
Funding
Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture

atopos project is an interdisciplinary theatre work at Art Space Mullae, Seoul, for which Gim directed the video. Taking atopos—Greek for “no place” or “impossible to categorize”—as its point of departure, and in dialogue with Judith Butler’s Gender Trouble and Julia Kristeva’s notion of poetic language, the production explores how performance produces meaning through instability, rhythm, and presence.

About

JH Gim (Jeonghwan Gim, b. 1996, Seoul) is an artist and filmmaker based between Vienna and Seoul. He works across moving image, performative installation, and sculptural arrangement. His practice examines how bodies and images are shaped by domestic and technical systems—from screens, furniture, and sound to infrastructures of measurement and display.

Treating images as spatial and behavioral conditions rather than representations, Gim constructs situations in which projection, reflection, ambient devices, and familiar objects choreograph attention. Across his works, support and dependency become unstable: bodies, objects, machines, and non-human actors sustain one another while also producing habit, pressure, and quiet constraint.
